The post Liquid AI Launches RIPL, a Real-Time Inference Engine for Sub-50 ms LFMs appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Liquid AI just announced Liquid RIPL , short for Real-time Inference Pipeline. RIPL is a low-latency engine that serves Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) inside a live request path. It returns complete generated responses end-to-end in under 50 ms. It also claims that latency holds while traffic arrives continuously at peak load. For developers, the message is simple. Swap gradient-boosted trees for a generative model, and keep the latency budget. TL;DR Engine : Serves LFM2.5 models from 230M to 2.6B parameters Runs on: Enterprise deployments on NVIDIA H100, H200, B200 and RTX PRO 6000 GPUs. Benchmarks used a single B200. Performance: 5.6 to 28.4x lower p95 latency than Qwen3.5 on vLLM, per Liquid’s own tests. Best: LFM2.5-1.2B hit 155.8 ms p95 vs 4,431 ms for Qwen3.5-0.8B, a 28.4x gap (256 in, 128 out). Worst: LFM2.5-2.6B gained only 5.6x (449.1 ms vs 2,499 ms). Sub-50 ms fails on longer requests. What problem does Liquid RIPL solve? Most serving stacks target large batches and long agentic jobs. A few seconds per request is acceptable there. Search ranking, fraud checks and payment authorization need answers in milliseconds. Liquid AI argues teams default to classical models for these paths because LLM serving is too slow. RIPL is built to remove that trade-off. How does RIPL work? Liquid AI describes RIPL as optimizing the full path, from request arrival to completed response. In several workloads, Liquid AI plots the same model, LFM2.5-350M, on vLLM and on RIPL. RIPL’s p95 line sits well below the vLLM line in each case. That isolates part of the gain to the engine, not just the model architecture. The LFM2.5 models themselves are hybrids. LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct has 16 layers: 10 double-gated convolution blocks and 6 GQA blocks. LFM2.5-2.6B has 30 layers: 22 convolution blocks and 8 GQA blocks. RIPL benchmarks: how fast is it vs vLLM? Liquid measured p95 end-to-end latency under open-loop Poisson arrivals on one B200. LFMs ran on RIPL. Baselines, including MiniCPM5 and Granite 4.2, ran on vLLM. The Gradium Phonon on-device TTS model comes in 31M and 40M sizes. The English Phonon 31m ships under Apache 2.0 and fits in a 64.5 MB file. Worst: 0.51% Seed-TTS LLM WER, behind Kokoro (0.45%) and Magpie (0.46%). What is Gradium Phonon? Phonon is an open-weight TTS family from Gradium , a Paris voice AI company spun out of Kyutai. It generates speech locally on phones, laptops, boards and browsers. The family has three models : Phonon 31m: English only, 37 built-in voices, Apache 2.0. Phonon 40m: 1 model per language (English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese), CC BY-NC 4.0. Phonon 40m multilingual: all 5 languages in 1 model, 102 voices, CC BY-NC 4.0. How does Phonon work? Phonon uses a causal transformer backbone. Its prefix combines text and speaker embeddings. A SentencePiece tokenizer with a 4,000-token vocabulary reads raw text, with no phoneme conversion. The backbone generates 1 latent vector per 80 ms frame. A flow-matching head turns that vector plus noise into an audio embedding in a single step. A smaller variant of Kyutai’s Mimi decoder then outputs 24 kHz PCM audio. A separate end-of-speech head decides when to stop. Phonon 31m uses 6 transformer layers, width 512 and 8 attention heads. The post TinyFish Breaks Down Agentic Search Architecture for Production AI Agents appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> An AI search agent can work in a demo but fail under production workloads when retrieval returns incomplete evidence, retries repeat unsuccessful actions, or execution exceeds time and cost limits. TinyFish , which provides web infrastructure for AI agents, has published two technical guides addressing these challenges. The first defines a production agentic search architecture , while the second shares lessons from building a deep research system . Together, they examine how an autonomous search agent can plan retrieval, evaluate evidence, handle failures, and manage the boundary between model reasoning and deterministic execution. TL;DR TinyFish introduced its agentic search architecture and key engineering lessons from building deep research systems. Built on four web primitives ( TinySearch, TinyFetch, TinyBrowser, and TinyAgent ), the system operates via a seven-phase control loop around the base model. On OpenBenchmarks, TinyFish achieved a 79.0% completion rate on coding tasks while delivering the lowest median task cost ($0.050) and token footprint, highlighting the importance of rigid control loops, failure-specific retries, and unified reasoning over standalone planners. What is Agentic Search Architecture? Agentic search architecture enables an AI agent to plan retrieval, access sources, evaluate evidence, and adapt its approach as new information becomes available. The model provides reasoning, while the surrounding application manages state, tool execution, evidence handling, runtime policies, and output validation. Together, these components allow an agent to handle incomplete results, recoverable failures, and changing information requirements. TinyFish’s architecture draws foundational concepts from a February 2026 architecture preprint , which decouples reasoning from execution through typed tool interfaces. The paper establishes essential system guardrails, including detailed tracing alongside strict caps on tokens, execution time, overall cost, and tool invocations. How does a production search run work? TinyFish splits a run into 7 phases: Define the task: Turn the goal into an “evidence contract”: required fields, sources, freshness and completion rules. Plan retrieval: Separate independent needs from dependent ones. Dependent queries wait for earlier answers. Pick the first route: Choose a tool based on what the system knows about the evidence. Discover, select, retrieve: Treat search results as candidates until the page content arrives. Evaluate: Label evidence as sufficient, incomplete, conflicting, inaccessible or budget exhausted. Recover or escalate: Revise the query, retry, change sources or change access method. Stop and validate: Return completed, incomplete, failed, cancelled or human review required. Phase 2 addresses a known failure. ChainRAG (ACL 2025) calls it the ‘lost-in-retrieval’ problem, where key entities disappear during multi-hop question decomposition. Phase 6 draws on Search-R1 , which demonstrates how models can learn to generate additional search queries during reasoning when earlier retrieval is insufficient. Across 7 QA datasets, its learned multi-turn search beat RAG baselines by 41% (Qwen2.5-7B) and 20% (Qwen2.5-3B). How should a search agent route tools? Routing should follow the information gap, not a fixed ladder. Starting condition Primitive What the app still owns Source location unknown Search Query planning, source policy, stopping URL known and readable Fetch Completeness checks, claim validation App must control page actions Browser Every action, retry and checkpoint Decisions across several pages Web Agent Business rules, budgets, validation Escalation is not always the fix. Weak results need a better query. Conflicting sources need stronger evidence. A heavier tool fixes neither. Retries should be based on the failure type and remain within defined limits. Transient errors may justify repeating a request, while incomplete or conflicting evidence requires a different approach. The deep research agent searches, browses, and generates comprehensive, cited reports. Most engineering challenges centered around context management, system orchestration, and product design. Lesson #1: Removing the separate planner Initial iterations used a standalone planner called fresh each time. Only structured state crossed into it. On follow-up queries like “focus only on pricing risks in Southeast Asia,” the agent drifted back to broad market research. TinyFish subsequently moved planning into the orchestrator’s own unified reasoning loop. Lesson #2: Removing subagents: TinyFish initially assigned a separate subagent to each search query, increasing context-switching overhead, latency, and cost. The team later replaced these subagents with tool calls for repeatable tasks such as ranking search results, classifying sources, and extracting evidence. This reduced the information passed back to the orchestrator, allowing it to focus on research

The role will involve working with GPU infrastructure for LLM workloads and ensuring systems can be deployed, monitored, and maintained reliably at scale.</p><p>The engineer should be comfortable troubleshooting infrastructure and deployment issues, automating deployment processes, and working with observability platforms such as Grafana and Prometheus.</p><p>Location: Riyadh, Saudi Arabia<br>Onsite requirement: A few times per quarter in Riyadh</p><p>Tasks and Deliverables</p><p>Design and support air-gapped deployment environments for LLM-based systems.</p><p>Deploy and optimize LLM workloads on GPU infrastructure.</p><p>Support large-scale software deployments across secure environments.</p><p>Implement and maintain observability using Grafana and Prometheus.</p><p>Collaborate onsite in Riyadh to assess, deploy, and troubleshoot environment-specific issues.</p><p>Required experience</p><p>Expertise in air-gapped deployments.</p><p>Experience with large-scale software deployments.</p><p>Experience deploying LLMs on GPUs.</p><p>Hands-on experience with Grafana and Prometheus.</p><p>Engagement highlights</p><p>Senior-level infrastructure/deployment engineering role.</p><p>Work on large-scale GPU and LLM infrastructure.</p><p>Challenging deployment scenarios involving air-gapped environments.</p><p>Full-time, long-term position</p> <p><strong>To apply:</strong> <a href="https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/toptal-senior-deployment-engineer-with-llm-and-gpu-infrastructure-experience">https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/toptal-senior-deployment-engineer-with-llm-and-gpu-infrastructure-experience</a></p> Thu, 22 Oct 2026 18:59:03 +0000 Sat, 21 Nov 2026 18:59:03 +0000 https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/toptal-senior-deployment-engineer-with-llm-and-gpu-infrastructure-experience https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/toptal-senior-deployment-engineer-with-llm-and-gpu-infrastructure-experience Toptal: AI Engineer - You can easily spot what works in content and what needs improvement.</p> </li> <li> <p>You know how to use AI effectively to create and edit content.</p> </li> <li> <p>You’re comfortable working with metrics and taking responsibility for content performance. oldContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Thu, 22 Oct 2026 14:12:42 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.11 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 Exclusive: Slingshot Raises $27M In Seed Funding To Build An Insurer For Those Small Policies Sold At Checkout https://news.crunchbase.com/fintech-ecommerce/insuretech/startup-slingshot-insurance-seed-funding-genteman/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 13:00:23 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94267 Slingshot Insurance , an AI-native embedded insurance startup, is emerging from stealth with $27 million in seed funding, it tells Crunchbase News exclusively. Rally Ventures and Skyward Group co-led the round, with participation from insurance industry veterans including Jim Hays , who will join Slingshot’s board. Rally is also a co-founder of the Minneapolis-based startup, as part of the firm’s broader approach. So far, it has co-founded roughly eight portfolio companies that have either launched or remain in stealth. Ethan Genteman, co-founder and CEO of Slingshot Insurance. (Courtesy photo) Slingshot, which is led by first-time founder and CEO Ethan Genteman , focuses on small insurance policies that consumers can buy as part of another purchase, such as coverage when booking a flight. Known as embedded insurance, the model puts coverage in front of customers when they might need it. The startup’s software helps businesses offer those policies by connecting them with insurers that back the coverage. It uses AI to process and share data between the two sides, aiming to reduce the administrative work that can make inexpensive policies costly to offer. Its first customer and design partner is Vertical Insure , which serves more than 750,000 customers at an average premium of $25, according to Slingshot. Genteman told Crunchbase News that Slingshot’s first program will launch this month. For now, Slingshot earns revenue as a technology provider working with outside insurers. But the six-person company, which formally began operating July 1, is also pursuing an acquisition that would allow it to back policies itself. “We’re not a carrier yet, but we are rapidly closing on our carrier,” Genteman said in an interview. Making the math work on a $25 policy One product Slingshot is working on would let parents buy insurance when signing a child up for youth sports, Genteman said. A parent spending $2,000 on a volleyball league, for example, might be offered a $25 policy covering cancellation or an injury during the season. Each policy includes paperwork and coordination with an insurer, and can bring potential claims. But when policies cost so little, managing them can quickly eat into the money they bring in, noted Genteman. He believes that as vertical SaaS companies increasingly look beyond traditional subscription fees for growth, embedded insurance is “a largely untapped opportunity” to generate incremental revenue from transactions already happening on their platforms while delivering additional value to customers. “The challenge is that the insurance and regulatory landscape is incredibly complex, and most SaaS companies don’t have the expertise, industry relationships or understanding of where to begin,” he said. Slingshot aims to solve this by providing a white-glove service for those vertical SaaS companies, helping them go from an insurance product idea to “a fully operational offering.” He offered a hypothetical example: A program collecting $500,000 in premiums with a 10% margin would have just $50,000 in margin. “That’s not a viable program for the way incumbent carriers have set themselves up operationally,” he said. Slingshot’s goal is to replace the spreadsheets, emails and disconnected systems used to manage that work with software that connects policy distributors and insurers directly. The company says its AI automates data-heavy tasks while keeping a record of decisions that the businesses involved can review and check. It charges a 5% technology fee to administer programs through its platform. Acquiring an insurer would let it provide both the software and the financial backing, according to Genteman. A customer helped shape the business The difficulties facing Slingshot’s first customer helped bring the startup together. Rally had already helped start Vertical Insure, which uses software platforms to sell insurance to its customers. According to Genteman, that business had opportunities to introduce more products but struggled to find insurers whose technology and processes could keep up. “We can design the products our customers need almost overnight, but the industry is highly regulated, and we need delegated authority just to write and distribute what we’ve built,” Vertical Insure co-founder and CEO Brock Noland said in a statement. “The antiquated approval process on the carrier-side slows everything down.” Even after finding an insurer willing to back a product, connecting the two companies’ systems could create more delays, Genteman said. Slingshot was built to address those problems, with Vertical Insure helping shape its product as a design partner. Noland is also a Slingshot co-founder. The opportunity in vertical SaaS Genteman sees a broader opening among vertical SaaS companies: businesses that sell software tailored to a particular industry. As vertical SaaS companies look for ways to grow beyond subscription fees, insurance could give them another avenue to make money from purchases customers already make through their platforms, argues Genteman. They already know their customers and what they’re buying, putting them in a position to offer coverage that fits the purchase. A babysitting platform, for example, could offer coverage to help parents pay for replacement childcare if a sitter cancels at the last minute. Software used by pet boarding facilities could offer coverage for unexpected vet bills if a pet is injured during a stay. An equipment rental platform could let customers add protection at checkout against accidental damage or theft. Those are examples of what could be developed, Genteman said. Slingshot aims to help vertical SaaS companies take ideas like those and turn them into insurance they can sell, providing both the software and help navigating the insurance industry and its regulatory requirements. “Insurance becomes another product that can be offered naturally within the existing customer experience,” he said. For Justin Kaufenberg , managing director at Rally Ventures, that opportunity is familiar. Before joining Rally, he ran SportsEngine , where insurance sold through its software became a key revenue source. “That experience gave me firsthand insight into the opportunity for software companies to generate revenue through embedded financial products,” he wrote via email. Kaufenberg sees similar potential across Rally’s portfolio, where most companies combine AI products with financial services. He said founders increasingly want insurance partners that can help them introduce coverage quickly. Rally co-founded Slingshot to bring insurance backing, underwriting, reporting, claims handling and distribution together in one business. “To get the carrier, the reinsurance, the underwriting platform, the data flow engine, the reporting capabilities, the claims handling, the embedded distribution engine, and every other part of the offering from a single vendor is unheard of,” Kaufenberg said. From insurance executive to founder Before starting Slingshot, Genteman was chief actuarial officer at publicly traded Palomar Holdings , where he also led data. He joined in 2019 and helped build its actuarial and data team as the company expanded beyond earthquake insurance into other coverage types. newContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Thu, 22 Oct 2026 15:38:48 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.11 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 Protecting Trade Secrets In The Age Of AI https://news.crunchbase.com/ai/protecting-trade-secrets-legal-kugler-grellas-shah/ Fri, 23 Oct 2026 11:00:29 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94271 By Seth Kugler If you only have six months of experience in an industry, you usually aren’t equipped to poach your employer’s clients and start a competing business. Of course, you may believe otherwise if you plan to use your employer’s proprietary information to train an AI agent to do the heavy lifting for you. Seth Kugler, partner at Grellas Shah LLP. That is exactly what the defendant attempted in a recent federal trade secrets case I litigated on behalf of a client in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. In that case, the defendant, a former senior employee at the marketing agency, didn’t just copy client lists to solicit accounts. Instead, he used stolen trade secrets as training inputs to build, essentially, an AI version of his old boss , attempting a shortcut to create a competing business without spending years developing the skills and expertise typically needed to provide such services. AI is creating new ways to misappropriate trade secrets, well beyond the classic theft story of an employee downloading files onto a thumb drive. This case highlights a new reality for founders, exposing unprecedented risks related to AI and trade secrets, employee use of personal devices, and the heightened need for companies to protect themselves in the age of agentic AI. Key lessons for founders AI contamination cannot be undone The defense in this case argued that because their client placed the stolen documents in a “quarantine folder” and no clients had been poached yet, no harm had been done. The court appropriately recognized that the “quarantine folder” was grossly insufficient, granting our temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction while recognizing the competing AI agent as an “existential threat.” An agreement not to touch just the stolen documents themselves is essentially irrelevant once AI gets involved: If a trade secret is used to develop a machine learning model or used to train an AI agent with recursive capabilities, it contaminates the model and the impact can be difficult to undo. Even if raw source files are completely scrubbed of any direct evidence of stolen materials, defendants will struggle to prove to courts that the AI isn’t operating a certain way precisely because it once had access to that proprietary information. Personal devices can pose big risks While trade secret misappropriation has typically been malicious, AI now also creates significant risks of inadvertent violations. Startups frequently scale with employees working on personal devices under standard Confidential Information and Invention Assignment Agreements. Running desktop AI agents on these devices can pose a serious risk. Unlike standard web interfaces, a desktop AI agent can scan files, create folders and ingest directory paths across a local hard drive, often without requiring special permission or alerting the user. Right now, thousands of employees may be inadvertently violating confidentiality agreements by running consumer AI agents on personal laptops that house their employers’ IP. If settings allow model training from this data, courts may eventually find these trade secrets to have lost legal protection due to dissemination outside the company. Standard IT audits won’t catch AI data theft This recent case serves as a warning for how attorneys and founders must approach trade secret investigations. Traditional digital discovery is no longer sufficient because AI tools make it effortless to disperse, alter and recreate data across nonobvious folder paths. Actions that previously seemed like overkill — such as full forensic imaging of a personal device — are now the bare minimum. Furthermore, AI dramatically reduces the friction of reverse-engineering software and tech products, potentially removing telltale signs that code or data was copied. Proving theft in AI contexts requires intensive, highly technical expert analysis and carries far more uncertainty than traditional IP litigation. 3 practical steps companies should take Founders should take three legal and operational steps to proactively protect their business: Implement strict agentic AI policies: Mandate tight controls and settings that isolate outside AI from company documents. Web-based tools like Claude with strict data privacy policies are vastly safer than open source or desktop apps that crawl local drives. Some AI agents should not be permitted to run at all within an environment containing trade secrets. Eliminate remote access from unmanaged devices: Shift to a closed cloud environment where data can be viewed and manipulated on a secure server, but files cannot be downloaded locally to a personal desktop. Removing local file downloads eliminates the risk of desktop AI agents indexing proprietary data. Rewrite your Confidential Information and Invention Assignment Agreements for the AI era: Standard confidentiality agreements need explicit clauses addressing AI use, model training inputs, and a precise definition of data misappropriation through machine learning. If you suspect an employee has walked away with data or misused it in an AI tool, your first step should be immediate: cut off all system access and retain counsel. Don’t wait until you start losing clients or experiencing financial losses. Feeding trade secrets into AI presents an existential threat from day one. AI gives individuals the unprecedented ability to compete in spaces where they lack experience, making proprietary data more vulnerable than ever. Modernizing security, policy and legal strategies to address today’s AI threats will help startups and established companies avoid catastrophic exposure. Seth Kugler is a partner at Grellas Shah LLP , where he focuses on complex commercial litigation, including disputes related to trade secret and IP misappropriation, corporate governance and breach of fiduciary duties, breach of contract, and other complex business disputes. He specializes in preventing and resolving all manner of disputes among and between corporate founders, directors, officers and shareholders, LLC members, and other current and former business partners.
